source.title: The exploding gradient problem demystified - definition, prevalence, impact, origin, tradeoffs, and solutions
source.authors: George Philipp; D. Song; J. Carbonell

record.file_problem: Full text is present; no relevant truncation or garbling identified.
record.tranche_reason: The study directly trains deep MLPs on CIFAR-10 and reports training classification errors that qualify the claim: some architectures train poorly, while initialization, normalization, and step-size choices substantially change the outcome.
record.gate_note: The paper reports CIFAR-10 training-error outcomes and random-initialization gradient measurements that bear on the listed versions. It also discusses cited work on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet; those cited outcomes are not extracted as this study's results. Values used only to select step sizes are not rows.
record.test_reason: The study tests initialization-dependent training in plain MLPs (V4), and reports a setting where batch normalization prevents learning (V6). Its MLP training errors do not test V1's convolutional-network claim. It does not conduct V3's comparison across training depths.
record.authors_conclusion: The record is broadly accurate but incomplete. The authors argue that relative gradient explosion and collapsing domains can both limit effective depth, and that stabilizing forward activation magnitudes does not generally solve these problems. They recommend an orthogonal initial state, approximated by residual shortcuts or looks-linear initialization; ordinary orthogonal weight initialization is a weaker strategy. They also emphasize layer-wise step sizes and tradeoffs between dilution and nonlinear representational capacity.
record.recipe_differences: The study analyzes MLP gradient scale and trains 51-linear-layer fully connected networks on CIFAR10 using SGD, Gaussian, orthogonal or looks-linear initialization, and custom or single step sizes; it does not reproduce the listed source recipes as a package.
record.method_sensitivity: Training outcomes vary with architecture, normalization, initialization, batch size, and single versus layer-wise step sizes. The batch-ReLU Gaussian model is especially sensitive to batch size: minibatch error remained above 89%, while the reported full-batch error was 34.83% with custom step sizes. Width 200 slightly reduced SELU gradient-explosion rate in the initialization analysis.

fits_no_version.finding: CIFAR-10 MLP training endpoints range from nearly zero to substantial error, depending on activation, normalization, skip connections and training recipe.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Depth-51 fully connected networks have strongly recipe-dependent training success on CIFAR-10.

fits_no_version.finding: Identity shortcuts reduce gradient growth and generally improve fixed-depth residual MLP training, with layer-SELU an exception.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Residual shortcuts mitigate gradient pathology in the tested MLPs; their benefit depends on architecture.

fits_no_version.finding: Initialization-only GSC, domain-collapse and effective-depth measurements describe gradient pathology rather than directly measuring training speed, classification fitting or stability-threshold recovery.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Stable activation magnitudes alone do not guarantee small relative gradients, preserved nonlinear representations or successful deep training.

record.problems: The CIFAR10 study is limited to MLPs, uses custom step-size selection procedures, disregards the test set, and reports no uncertainty estimates. Some table entries for the leaky-ReLU sweep are flattened and difficult to map reliably.
record.rows_left_out: Rows R1-R60 exhaust the 60-row limit. The source table also includes additional leaky-ReLU and batch-leaky-ReLU leakage-sweep values; those entries cannot be reliably mapped from the supplied flattened table, so they are not assigned additional rows. The table's aggregate summary is retained where apparent mapping is possible.

untested.parts: Not tested: all experiments use fully connected MLPs, not convolutional networks; no CIFAR-100 or corrupted-label training.
No teacher-student problem, spurious-minimum frequency, or student-versus-teacher width comparison.
No convolutional-network training-depth sweep or longer-training comparison; fixed-depth residual MLP comparisons do not establish depth degradation. No Xiao or Fixup recipe.

No direct orthogonal-versus-Gaussian tanh training-speed experiment, controlled training-depth sweep, or 10,000-layer convolutional experiment. Table 1's orthogonal tanh measurements involve no training.
No initial linearized stability threshold, catapult, sharpness trajectory, or edge-of-stability experiment.
No controlled higher-learning-rate tolerance comparison, original sigmoid/VGG/Inception setting, or Fixup experiment. Normalization omits trainable shifts and scales.

missing.what: Separate minibatch Gaussian batch-ReLU failure: training error remains above 89%, compared with 90% random guessing. Existing rows record only full-batch endpoints.

Initialization-dependent training trajectories and GSC during training, needed to distinguish learning speed from final error. Looks-linear initialization suppresses batch-ReLU gradient growth throughout training.

Training comparisons underlying the authors' qualification of edge-of-chaos initialization guidance: with layer-wise step sizes, chaotic SELU and layer-tanh outperform edge-of-chaos ReLU, layer-ReLU and tanh. This is a recipe-dependent comparison, not an isolated initialization experiment.

record.verdict_notes: This study is not an original source for any listed version. Table 2 can be reconstructed by aligning its 33 entries across columns; the record invents many additional results and repeatedly assigns the final 54.64% entry to unrelated conditions. Reported training endpoints are selected over step-size searches, with termination after 500 epochs or 11 reductions. A corrected value's cannot_determine state means it cannot establish the linked claim effect, not that the endpoint itself is unreadable.

versions.untested_parts: CIFAR-100, corrupted or random labels, convolutional networks, Adam, and smaller-model or early-stopping comparisons are not tested.
The paper does not study two-layer ReLU teacher-student local minima or student width relative to teacher width.
The paper does not compare plain and residual convolutional networks across depth on ImageNet or CIFAR-10, or test the cited special plain-network and normalization-free recipes as stated.

The paper compares Gaussian, orthogonal and looks-linear initializations in its MLP experiments, but does not test the cited activation-matched initialization claims across plain feedforward depths, orthogonal versus Gaussian deep tanh learning speed, or 10,000-layer convolutional networks.
No above-stability learning-rate catapult or edge-of-stability experiment is conducted.
The paper tests batch normalization in deep MLP architectures on CIFAR-10, not sigmoid MNIST, VGG CIFAR-10 or Inception ImageNet accuracy speed or learning-rate tolerance; it does not test Fixup.
